title: The 3-2-1 backup rule: why one copy is never enough

audience.who: corporate employees, mostly non-technical, who keep work files on a laptop
audience.knows: that backups exist; assumes a file saved on the laptop or synced somewhere is safe
audience.cares_about: not losing a week of work or a deliverable the day before it is due

outcome: After watching, you can look at where your important work files live, say whether they would survive a dead drive, a stolen bag or ransomware, and fix the gap with three copies, on two kinds of storage, one kept offsite.
through_line: One copy is a single point of failure; each extra copy guards against a different way of losing it, so the rule is not about having more copies but about copies that cannot all fail together.

arc_plan.what: One work file, the only copy, on one laptop the day before it is due; the drive fails. The viewer recognises the assumption that the file is simply there.
A three-number rule makes that loss survivable: 3-2-1.
Three copies: the original plus two backups, so one failure never leaves zero.
Two kinds of storage: copies on different media or devices, so one fault cannot take them all.
One offsite: a copy kept somewhere else, commonly the cloud, so fire, theft or ransomware in one place leaves a copy untouched.
The viewer judges a setup (laptop plus a USB drive carried in the same bag) and spots which part of the rule it breaks.
Back to the opening file: the same failure strikes and the work survives because the rule is in place.

must_cover.what: The 3-2-1 rule: three copies of the data, on two different types of storage, with one copy offsite
A single copy is a single point of failure (hardware failure, loss or theft, accidental deletion, ransomware)
Copies kept on the same device or in the same place can be lost together
Cloud storage as a common way to keep the offsite copy

must_avoid: statistics on data loss or drive failure rates without a source
naming or endorsing specific backup vendors or products
deep technical detail (RAID, backup software settings, incremental versus full backups)
opening by explaining the term or listing an agenda
a presenter or person on screen: the requester asked for pure motion graphics
example_posture: One running example the whole lesson returns to: a single work file (a report) on an employee's laptop, followed through a copy, a second device, the cloud, and a failure it survives. Ordinary office situations, no hacker drama.
visual_direction: Pure motion graphics on the style's plain light field, the system itself in motion: the file as a clear object copied to a second device and to the cloud, one copy visibly placed offsite, a failure shown and survived. Crisp shapes, clear labels, purposeful motion; each of the rule's three numbers shown large when named and tied to its picture.
voice_note: A capable colleague who has watched someone lose a week of work: calm, practical, a little dry. No scare tactics, no lecturing.
open_questions: Does the organisation already back up laptops centrally? The lesson stays general and about personal practice unless told otherwise.
